Updated 19 August 2026
Open the CRM

Start here

This tool answers one question: what needs a follow-up today? That is the whole job. If you only ever open the Today screen each morning and work down it, you are using it correctly.

It exists because things slip. Not because anyone is careless — because a promise made on a call at 16:40 on a Thursday lives in your head, and then in nobody's. This is where you put it so it comes back to you.

Three things that are always true

  1. Nothing is ever blocked. There is no required field, no form you must finish, no dialog you must clear. If you want to record half a thing and move on, you can.
  2. Nothing is ever hidden. If you push a date, it says so. If a deal has no next move, it gets its own section. The tool does not tidy away the awkward bits.
  3. You can always say "not now" — you just also have to say "then when".

It takes about ten minutes to learn. Read Your morning and Logging what happened; the rest you can look up when you need it.

Your morning

Open the app. You land on Today. It has three sections, always in the same order.

1 · Overdue

Things you said you'd do, on a date that has already passed. A red edge, and it tells you exactly how late it is and how many times it has been moved.

Work these first. That is why they are at the top.

2 · Due today

What you scheduled for today. Blue edge. Clear it and the day is done.

3 · No next step

This is the section that makes this tool different from a to-do list, so it is worth thirty seconds.

These are open deals where nobody has agreed what happens next. Not late — unscheduled. A normal task list can't show you this, because a task nobody wrote down looks exactly like a clear day.

It is drawn with no colour and a dashed outline on purpose. That grey hatched strip is the space where the next step should be. It is meant to look like something is missing, because something is.

A deal sitting here isn't a telling-off. It usually means a conversation ended without a clear next move — which happens constantly. The fix takes five seconds: click Set next step, say what you'll do, pick a date.

Mine and Team

Top right. Mine is your day and it's the default. Team shows everyone's, so a colleague's account going quiet is visible to more than one person. Nobody is being monitored; the point is that a deal shouldn't go silent just because one person was on leave.

Working a row

  • Done — you did it. The row folds away and the count drops by one. You'll then be asked what's next on that deal.
  • Defer — not today. Pick a new date.
  • Click the row itself — opens the deal, with its full history.

Logging what happened

Every flag, every reminder, every "this account has gone quiet" in this tool is calculated from what you log. If it isn't logged, the tool is confidently wrong about that account. This is the one habit worth building.

The good news: it's designed to take about fifteen seconds, it's two keystrokes from anywhere in the app, and it saves the moment you press Save. The "what's next?" question comes after, and you can ignore it.

The fastest route: press l

From anywhere in the app — Today, Pipeline, Week, doesn't matter — press l. You don't have to find the deal first.

  1. Press l (or click Log in the top right).
  2. The list is already showing what's on your plate today, so often the one you want is right there. Otherwise type a company, deal or person's name — searching for Thandi finds Sandton's deals, because you remember people, not deal names.
  3. ↑ ↓ then Enter, or just click.
  4. Pick the kind, check the date, type one line, Save.

This is the habit worth building. Two keystrokes from anywhere. If logging is a chore you have to navigate to, it doesn't happen — and then everything else in here is quietly wrong.

A phone call — the everyday case

  1. Press l and pick the customer.
  2. Pick Call. Today's date is already filled in.
  3. Type one line: what was actually said or agreed.
  4. Save.

If you already have the deal open on screen, l skips the picker and logs straight against it.

Write the line for the person who reads it in six weeks. "Spoke to Thandi" tells you nothing later. "Thandi wants two clauses changed before legal will sign" tells you exactly where you are.

A WhatsApp conversation

There are two ways, and the quick one is right most of the time.

Quick way — for a short exchange

Don't bother exporting anything. Open the deal, Log an interaction, choose WhatsApp, set the date if it wasn't today, and type your one line. Same as a phone call. Ten seconds.

Full way — paste the actual chat

Worth it when the conversation ran over several days and you want the dates right, or when you want it filed against the correct contact automatically.

First, get the chat out of WhatsApp. On your phone:

  • iPhone — open the chat, tap the contact's name at the top, scroll down, tap Export Chat, choose Without Media.
  • Android — open the chat, tap the ⋮ menu top right, then More › Export chat, choose Without media.

Send it to yourself (email, or your own notes) and open the .txt file. If WhatsApp has moved that menu since this was written, look for anything called Export — the file it produces is what matters, not the route.

Then, in the CRM:

  1. Open the deal the conversation belongs to.
  2. Click Paste a chat or email.
  3. Paste the whole thing in. Don't tidy it up.

It reads the chat and tells you what it found — that it's WhatsApp, how many messages, who with, and the date of the most recent one. Nothing is saved yet.

  1. Click Use this.
  2. The log form opens with WhatsApp already selected and the date already set from the conversation.
  3. Replace the summary with your own line and Save.

The summary it suggests is deliberately useless. It says "WhatsApp with Thandi Mokoena · 4 messages" and nothing about what was discussed — because the app never reads the content of your messages back to you or anyone else. That one line is yours to write. Write a real one.

An email

Exactly the same route — Paste a chat or email — but paste the email instead. The From, Date and Subject lines are enough; you don't need the body. It works out who sent it, matches them to a contact, and fills in the date.

To email someone from here: open the deal, and their address in the Contacts section is a link that opens your normal mail app.

Meetings, and everything else

There are six kinds in total. Call, WhatsApp and Email you'll use most; the other three matter more than they look.

  • LinkedIn — where a good many introductions actually start, and where some of them stay. Filing one as a note loses the single fact that explains an empty mailbox: the conversation was never in email.
  • Meeting — anything face to face or on a video call. Worth logging even when nothing was decided, because "we met and it went nowhere" is real information.
  • Note — for what you learn without a conversation. They're restructuring. A competitor is in there. Their FD leaves in March. Someone mentioned a budget freeze at a conference.

A note counts as contact. The Silent 30d flag looks at anything logged, of any kind — so a note stops the clock the same way a call does. Don't use one to make an account look busier than it is; you'll only be lying to yourself in six weeks.

What actually gets saved

Staff ask this, and they should. When you paste a conversation:

SavedNot saved — ever
  • That it was a WhatsApp / email / call
  • The date it happened
  • Who it was with
  • Which deal it belongs to
  • The one line you typed
  • The messages themselves
  • Any part of what was said
  • The pasted text, in any form

The paste is read inside your own browser and thrown away the moment you click Use this. It is never sent anywhere and never written down. This is a deliberate design decision, not a limitation: records here are kept permanently, and a customer's private messages should not be.

Which means the one line you type is the record. It's the only thing anyone will have.

If it says it can't find a match

The app matches a conversation to a contact by email address, by the name the chat is saved under, or by phone number. If none of those are on file it will say no match.

The fix: open the right deal first, then click Paste a chat or email from inside it. Pasting from within a deal files it against that deal regardless. If it notices the conversation looks like it belongs to a different company, it will warn you in red — read that before you save.

If a paste isn't recognised at all, it tells you what it was looking for. Free text you typed yourself won't parse — just use Log an interaction instead.

The next step

After you log something, you get asked this:

Type what you'll do next, tap a date, done. 1 tomorrow, 3 three days, 7 a week, 4 a fortnight — or type a date in your own words: fri, +21, 3 sep, 2026-09-03.

The quick buttons skip weekends. +3 days from a Wednesday lands on Monday, not Saturday. A date you type yourself is left exactly as you typed it — if you want Saturday, you can have Saturday.

"No next step yet"

That button is there on purpose and it is not a failure. Sometimes you genuinely don't know — you're waiting on their board, their budget, their new FD to start.

Click it, and the deal drops into the No next step section on Today, where you and everyone else can see it. That is the honest outcome. What it will not do is quietly disappear.

It's still better to put a placeholder date on it — "check in after their year end", 30 September — because then it comes back to you on its own instead of relying on someone spotting it.

Deferring

Move anything, as often as you like. No reason required, no limit, nobody approves it.

But every move is counted, and the row shows it: pushed 4× · originally due 26 Jul.

That counter isn't there to catch you out. It's there because "I'll get to it tomorrow" four times in a row is a completely different situation from "I moved it once", and after a fortnight neither you nor anyone else can tell the two apart from memory. A deal you've pushed five times is usually a deal that needs a different conversation, not a later one.

Deals

Adding one

Press n, or click New deal top right.

Company and deal name are all you really need. Value and expected close date can wait — but if you know them, put them in, because they're what the forecast is built from.

Note the First next step field. Every new deal is created with one. You can't accidentally create a deal that nobody ever follows up.

Moving a deal along

Four stages: Lead → Qualified → Proposal → Negotiation, then Won or Lost.

On the Pipeline screen, drag a card between columns. Or open the deal and change the dropdown in its header. Same thing.

Each card shows the next step at the bottom. If it's late it goes red; if there isn't one, you get the hatched no next step strip again.

There is no "on hold" stage, deliberately. Deals go into a parked column and never come out — it looks tidy and quietly becomes where deals go to die. Park a deal by giving it a next step with a date far out instead. It stays open, it stays yours, and it comes back on its own.

Closing one

Open the deal, click Won or Lost in the header. Lost asks for a reason — optional, but worth it; it's the only place that knowledge survives.

Closing a deal stops it asking for next steps. That's the point: the nagging ends when the deal genuinely ends.

Partners, and people who become companies

Some of what we sell reaches the customer through somebody else. Open the company and click mark as a partner — you can do this before they have brought anything in, which is usually when you want to, because a partnership being negotiated is exactly the thing that gets forgotten.

Once a company is a partner it appears in the Via partner box when you edit a deal. The deal still belongs to the customer; the partner box only records who brought it. A company can never be its own partner.

A bucket that holds individuals can't be a partner — it isn't one organisation, it's a drawer full of private buyers.

When a person turns into a company. Someone enquires as themselves, then forms an entity, or reopens one they had closed. Edit the deal and change Filed under. Everything logged against the deal goes with it — every interaction, every follow-up, every invoice. You'll be offered the chance to move that person's contact record across as well; anyone else in the bucket stays where they are, and the form tells you how many that is.

An email batch can do the same move without anyone opening the deal: a row that names a different company is reported as a filed under change, alongside the row's own note about who moves and who stays, and nothing happens until you press Apply these deal changes. This is also the only way to bring a brand-new company into the CRM without raising a deal against it first.

Merging two records of one company

Two records for the same customer is a mistake, not a fact. Open the company, click merge…, pick the one to keep. Deals, people and everything logged move across.

Don't merge a customer into its partner. If Gary at a reseller brought you a bank's tender, the deal belongs to the bank — the reseller goes in the Via partner box on the deal. Merging them makes the reseller the customer and the bank stops existing, so your pipeline lists the people who introduced the work instead of the people buying it. The form warns you when it spots this.

Nothing is destroyed and you can always change your mind. A merge only sets a marker. Merged records are listed at the bottom of the Companies page under Merged away, each with put back — which returns the company, its deals and the partner that was recorded against them. Weeks later, still works.

Background — what's standing true

Some things about a customer aren't events. "They handle marketing and sales for us in the Gulf." "Purchase orders have to quote the contract number." That didn't happen on a Tuesday and it doesn't age, so logging it as an interaction is wrong — it would start the contact clock on something that never happened.

Put it in Background instead. Deals have one, in the edit form. Companies have one too — open the company and click add background. It shows above the log, because it's what you need before any of the events make sense.

Rule of thumb: the log is what happened; background is what is true. If it has a date, log it.

The deal screen

Slides in over whatever you were doing, so you never lose your place. Value and dates at the top, the open next step, then everything that has ever happened on this deal in date order, then the contacts.

If it has any flags, they're listed with the rule that triggered each one, so a flag is never mysterious.

Companies

Every company is a card, and the cards start shut. Click the name to open one; click again to shut it. The app remembers which you left open, so the page keeps its shape when you come back. Expand all is there when you want the lot, and the filter box narrows to a handful and opens them for you.

The line that stays visible

A shut card still tells you how you're doing with that customer:

  • Lifetime — cash that has actually arrived, read off payments against invoices. Not what has been sold, and not what has been invoiced. Those are different numbers and they get their own lines.
  • Owed — invoiced and not yet paid. In red, because it is the number that makes you pick up the phone.
  • In play — value sitting on open deals.
  • Chance — how likely a win is. See the warning below.
  • Closing — the earliest expected close date on an open deal, red if it has already gone past.
  • Logged and Last contact — how much has been recorded, how much of it was email, and how long ago.

"Chance" is the stage's number, not a judgement about the customer. It comes straight from the probability set against each stage in config.json — the same figure the forecast uses. Nobody scores individual deals here, deliberately: per-deal odds are where a number stops being a fact and becomes a mood. Where a company has open deals at several stages you'll see Furthest instead, and opening the card lists them all. There is no single blended company percentage, because averaging across currencies would need an exchange rate and the CRM does not invent one.

Open the card for the rest

Lifetime value, invoiced, outstanding, won-by-deal-value, open value, the deal counts, and the channel breakdown — then the deals, the people, the background, and everything ever logged against the company across all its deals.

Under the figures you may see a line beginning "Not counted above…". That is the CRM naming what it could not add up: deals carrying no value, work won that was never invoiced, deals with no expected close date. Read it. A total that quietly skipped those would look like a fact and be a guess.

Handing the CRM over

Sometimes something outside the app needs to know what the CRM currently holds — the email triage, an audit, a stand-in while you're away. There is one file for that.

Export the log

  1. Press g then s, or click Settings.
  2. Scroll to the import and export buttons.
  3. Click Export the raw event log.

You get crm-events-<date>.jsonl in your Downloads folder. That is everything: every person's events already merged, plus a first line carrying the roster, the stages and the build that wrote it. One file, not two. Nothing else needs to go with it.

Your GitHub token is not in it. The token and the configuration are separate things inside the app and the export only takes the configuration — there's a test that plants a fake token next to it and checks it doesn't come out. The file does contain customer names, deal values and commission figures, so treat it the way you'd treat the repo itself.

Knowing where you got to

Under the two import boxes the panel says when a batch was last imported, how many interactions landed in it, and who ran it — counted from the log itself, so it cannot drift from what is actually in there. Under the export buttons it says when this browser last took a copy.

Those two lines are worded differently on purpose. An import writes to the record, so the record knows. An export only reads, so it leaves no trace — the app can tell you what this browser did and honestly cannot tell you whether somebody exported the log from another machine. It says so rather than guessing.

This matters most in the middle of a run. A batch whose deals do not exist yet has to go in twice, so a morning's triage is often several files each imported twice. Without a line saying where you got to, the only way to check was to open a deal and try to remember whether that entry had been there before.

It's a photograph, not a window

An export is true at the moment you take it. Anything logged afterwards isn't in it. Take a fresh one each time rather than re-sending last week's — a stale export folds into something that looks exactly like a live CRM, which is the dangerous part.

Getting it back in

The same file imports: Settings → the import box. Events are keyed by id and the fold is last-write-wins, so importing the same file twice changes nothing. That's what makes it safe to hand around.

Week

Press g then w. Two halves on one page: what actually happened last week, and what the open pipeline is worth.

Last week — the retrospective

Counted from the log, Monday to Sunday: Follow-ups completed, Follow-ups pushed, New follow-ups created, Interactions logged, and Won value.

It tells you plainly when more was pushed than finished. That isn't a scolding — a week where everything moved a fortnight to the right is a real fact about the week, and it's the one a summary would normally round away.

Deals that lost their next step lists deals that ended the week with nothing scheduled. If it's empty it says so, rather than showing a blank space you have to interpret.

Forecast

Every open deal that carries a value, multiplied by the probability set for its stage, grouped by expected close month. Columns: Deals, Gross, Weighted.

Two things this deliberately won't do.

It never converts currencies. Rands and dollars are reported side by side and never added. A blended number needs an exchange rate with a date on it — that's a decision, not a default, and an invented one produces a confidently wrong figure.

Probabilities are fixed per stage in config.json and cannot be edited per deal. A per-deal slider is where a forecast stops being a measurement and becomes a mood.

Under the total, the page states how much of its own weighted value sits on deals whose expected close date has already passed, or that have no date at all. Read that line before you quote the total. A forecast where a third of the value is already overdue is not the same number as one where none of it is, and the total alone can't tell you which you're holding.

People

Press g then u, or click People. Pick a person from the row at the top and the page below is entirely theirs.

The Mine / Team toggle on Today answers "is this mine?" — the question you ask about your own day. This page answers a different one: how is one particular person doing?

Both halves of what somebody carries

Owning a deal and owning the next step on it are not the same thing, and the gap between them is where the real workload hides. So the page shows both:

  • Their deals — open, won, lost, value in play, what's outstanding, commission earned and pending.
  • Steps they're carrying on other people's deals — real work that no other screen shows, because every other screen keys on who owns the deal.
  • Steps on their deals that somebody else is holding — the same fact from the other side, so you can see what they're waiting on.

Someone can own no deals at all and still be carrying several overdue steps. Everybody on the roster gets a page, sellers or not — hiding the people who own nothing is exactly how their work goes missing.

"Logged by" is not a performance measure. It counts who typed the interaction in. If one person runs the email import, the whole team's correspondence is logged under their name. The page says so under the number, every time. Don't read it as a leaderboard.

Seeing every screen as one person

Picking somebody here does more than fill in this page. It sets a lens: Today, Pipeline, Companies, Week and Money all start answering for them instead of you. The row of buttons under the picker takes you straight to any of them.

You will always know it is on. A tinted banner sits next to the page title reading Viewing and then that person’s name, the Mine switch stops saying "Mine" and says their name instead, and the banner carries a Back to yours button. Reading somebody else’s overdue list and thinking it is your own is worse than not being able to read it at all, so the app would rather shout.

A lens changes what you see. It never changes who you are. Anything you log, complete or defer while looking at Thabo’s book is still written as you, into your own file. The CRM has exactly one writer per person and that does not bend. If something genuinely needs to be recorded as Thabo, Thabo records it.

Companies narrows to the companies that person has deals at, and says how many of the total that is, with a Show all companies button beside it. Settings never takes a lens — it configures the app, not anybody’s book.

A lens does not survive a reload. Close the tab and come back tomorrow and you are on your own list again. A lens you had forgotten about is a trap, so it only lasts as long as the banner announcing it.

When the roster and the data disagree

If config.json doesn't list someone as sales but deals are filed to them, the page says so in red. Commission is computed from that setting, so one of the two is wrong. Same if someone owns work and isn't in the roster at all — they get a page, marked not in the roster, because a person the CRM can't name is the one you most need to see.

Money

Press g then m, or click Money. Invoices and payments are entered on the deal itself, under Money; this screen adds them all up.

Winning is not being paid

Selling stops at Won. What happens afterwards — raising the invoice, chasing it, banking it — is a separate life the deal goes on having. Keeping the two apart is what stops the pipeline lying in both directions: revenue that hasn't arrived counted as if it had, and work delivered months ago still sitting in Negotiation.

So the screen shows four different numbers and never merges them: invoiced, paid, outstanding and overdue. Amounts are never converted between currencies and never added across them — a dollar total and a rand total sit side by side, because the only way to combine them is to invent an exchange rate.

Raising an invoice

Open the deal, then Raise invoice. Three amounts matter:

  • Net — the invoice excluding VAT.
  • VAT — added on for what the customer owes, and excluded from commission.
  • of which resale — the part of the net you are collecting for somebody else. It sits inside the net, not on top of it.

Commission is worked out on net minus resale, and is earned only once an invoice is settled in full. A percentage of a part-payment is a number somebody has to claw back later.

A due date is optional and worth filling in: without one, nothing can ever call the invoice late, and the app says so rather than quietly leaving it out.

When one invoice on a deal earns nobody

Commission is agreed per deal, but a deal can bill two different things. MCB's training earns 20%; the DMBOKs invoiced alongside it earn nobody anything, because the books are a publisher's.

Leave Commission % on this invoice empty and it follows the deal — the box tells you which rate that is. Put 0 in it and that one invoice earns nothing, while the deal stays where it was.

The invoice row then reads nothing rather than a currency amount, and says 0%, not 20% underneath it — both what this invoice pays and what it would have paid — so the zero reads as a decision rather than a missing figure. The Money heading on the deal warns that some invoices differ. Clearing the box puts the invoice back under the deal.

0% and resale are not the same claim. Resale says this money isn't really ours — we collect it and pass it on. 0% says the money is ours, but nobody earns on it. Both produce no commission, and only one of them is true of any given line. If the publisher invoices us and we bill it on at cost, that's resale. If we buy the books and sell them at a margin we keep, that's 0%.

Three ways money goes quiet

The Money screen collects the flags a closed deal can still carry: No invoice logged on work already won, Payment overdue, and No due date on something unpaid. Winning releases you from having a next step. It doesn't release you from getting paid.

Finding things

Press / anywhere. Type part of a company, deal or person's name.

Arrow keys to move, Enter to open. It's almost always faster than clicking through the Pipeline.

Companies in the left menu lists every account with all its deals, contacts and history in one place — useful before a meeting where you'll cover more than one thing.

On your phone

The same link works. Today is designed to be usable standing in a car park after a meeting, which is exactly when you should be logging it.

Done and Defer sit on every row without needing to hover. Log the call before you drive off — it takes fifteen seconds and it is the difference between this tool being right and being decoration.

Flags

Small grey and red chips on deals. Each is a plain rule, worked out fresh every time you open the app — never stored, never a score, never a judgement.

ChipWhat it means
Never contacted The deal exists but nothing has ever been logged against it.
No next step Open, but nobody has said what happens next.
Overdue A follow-up was due before today.
Pushed 3+ Moved three or more times. Worth a look.
Silent 30d Nothing logged for thirty days.
Stalled Sat in the same stage for forty-five days.
Close date passed Still open, but its expected close date is in the past. Update the date.
No invoice logged Won, with no invoice entered here. It may already be raised in your accounting system — this flag says the CRM has not been told, and until it is, nothing tracks whether you get paid.
Payment overdue An invoice is past its due date with money still outstanding.
No due date An unpaid invoice has no due date, so nothing can ever call it late.

On the Pipeline screen you can click any chip along the top to see only the deals carrying it. Good for a ten-minute tidy-up on a Friday.

The last three are about money rather than selling, and they are the only flags a closed deal can carry. Winning a deal releases you from having a next step; it does not release you from getting paid. They are collected on the Money screen — see below.

"Silent 30d" only knows what you've logged. If you've been talking to them weekly and not writing it down, the flag will be wrong — and so will everything else. It isn't the tool being stupid; it's the tool telling you the truth about what it was told.

Shortcuts

Worth learning four of these. The rest are there when you want them.

/Search — the one to learn first
lLog an interaction — from anywhere. Learn this one.
nNew deal
dMark the highlighted row done
1 3 7 4 Defer by 1, 3, 7 or 14 days
eDefer to a date you type
j kMove down and up the Today list
g then tGo to Today
g then pGo to Pipeline
g then cGo to Companies
g then wGo to Week
g then sGo to Settings
EscClose whatever is open

Dates accept: today, tom, fri, +21, 3 sep, 2026-09-03, 03/09/2026 (day first, as we write it here).

Questions we expect

I logged something on the wrong deal.

Open the right deal and log it again properly. The wrong one stays in the history — nothing here is deleted, by design, so the record is trustworthy. Add a note saying it was logged in error if it matters.

Can my manager see everything I do?

Yes, and so can you see theirs — it's one shared set of records. That's the point: a deal shouldn't go quiet just because one person was away. Nothing is tracked about you; it's about the accounts.

I've got twelve overdue items and it's depressing.

Take fifteen minutes and go down the list deciding one thing per row: do it, move it to a date you actually believe, or close the deal. A list that reflects reality is useful even when it's long. A list you're avoiding isn't.

Do I have to fill in the value and close date?

No. Nothing is required. But those two fields are the entire forecast, so if they're blank or stale the forecast is fiction — and someone will read it out in a meeting.

It says "Demo workspace" at the bottom left.

You're in the practice copy — invented companies, nothing real, nothing saved anywhere. Good for trying things. Ask Howard to point you at the team workspace when you're ready.

It says storage is full, or that it isn't saving.

The app itself uses very little — a few hundred kilobytes even after months of use. So "full" almost never means you have outgrown it. Two things cause it:

  • You opened the file directly from your computer rather than from its web address. Browsers lump every local file into one shared, unreliable storage area, and some give local files none at all. This is the usual cause. Fix: open the app from its web link, not by double-clicking a downloaded copy.
  • You're in a private / incognito window. Nothing is kept there by design. Use a normal window.

Go to Settings and look at This device. It tells you plainly whether saving works, where you opened the app from, how much the app is using, and what the browser's actual limit is. There are buttons there to free space and to export everything.

If you see the red "not saving" strip in the sidebar, act on it before you close the tab. Click Export now — that downloads everything as a file you can hand back. While that strip is showing, anything you log is only in the open tab.

Which version am I on?

Bottom left, under your name — something like v1.1.0 · 416723f3. Quote that if you report a problem; it says exactly which copy you're looking at.

If you're told to update, reload the page. If the version doesn't change, do a hard reload: Ctrl+Shift+R on Windows, ⌘+Shift+R on a Mac. Your work is safe — it lives in the shared repository, not in the page.

Something's wrong / it did something odd.

Tell Howard what you were doing when it happened, roughly when, and the version from the bottom-left corner. Every action is recorded, so it can be traced.

Nothing in the guide matches that.
